question: Two Wi-Fi networks in the list show the exact same name. What does that tell you?

options.text: Nothing unusual, it's completely normal
One of them is very likely fake, though the name alone won't tell you which
The one with the stronger signal is always the real one
It means the venue has excellent coverage

explanation: A network name proves nothing about who actually controls it — an attacker can broadcast an identical name right next to the real one, and most devices only show the name, not who set it up.

question: What is a "man-in-the-middle" position?

options.text: When two people are on a phone call together
When an attacker's device sits between you and the internet, able to see everything you send
A type of computer virus
A firewall configuration setting

explanation: Connecting to a rogue hotspot routes all your traffic through the attacker's device first — websites still load normally, but everything passes through them on the way.

question: You're about to log into a work account, and the address bar starts with "http://" instead of "https://". What should you do?

options.text: Proceed anyway, it's probably fine
Stop — without HTTPS, anything typed on the page can be read by others on the network
Just switch to a different browser
Refresh the page and try again

explanation: HTTPS encrypts what you send so only the real destination can read it. Without it, on an untrusted network, anything typed — including passwords — can potentially be intercepted in plain text.

question: What's the safest way to handle sensitive accounts while on public Wi-Fi?

options.text: Use a VPN, or avoid sensitive logins on public networks entirely
Turn on airplane mode first
Use an unusually long password just for that session
Ask venue staff which network is the "safe" one to log into things on

explanation: A VPN encrypts your traffic even if the network itself isn't trustworthy — the next best option is simply not logging into anything sensitive until you're on a network you actually trust.

question: Why is rogue-hotspot interception so hard to notice while it's happening?

options.text: It makes your phone vibrate unusually
Websites still load completely normally, with no visible error
It changes your device's wallpaper
It drains your battery instantly

explanation: There's no popup or crash — everything appears to work exactly as expected. The only real clue is usually something you'd have to check for yourself, like the missing padlock/HTTPS in the address bar.
